from White Wolf's site, current card text (as reprinted in Sabbat War):

Name: Legacy of Pander
Cardtype: Political Action

Political Card-Worth 1 Vote. Called by any Sabbat vampire at +1 stealth.
If this referendum is successful, put this card in play. Each non-titled
Pander has one vote. Any Sabbat vampire may call a referendum to burn this
card as a +1 stealth political action.

Note that it says "one vote" now, not "one additional vote".

> common thread on new errata, and it doesn't make me happy. It's just
> a different form of card-limits.

Making a card non-stackable COMPLETELY and TOTALLY fails to resemble
anything to do with card limits. You can put as many LoP in your deck as
you want, and put as many in play as you want, and each one must be burned
by a separate action. You just can't stack them up to have a weenie
powerhouse vote machine anymore. Corresponding examples: A vampire may
have no more than one Disarm, and you can still put 12 of them in your deck
(probably quite effectively). You can no longer play more than one DotB
per combat, and it's STILL worth putting a bunch in.

You would also consider the original Army of Rats errata bad?

> Dont be using logic now to argue. Of course, some people object to an
> oldschool 'Legacy' Deck, but think Majesty decks are fair. We dont get

Way to shoot yourself in the foot there, guy. Experience and evidence have
demonstrated conclusively that Majesty is, in fact, totally non-broken AND
fair at this time. A quick review of the decks in the Continental
Championship final (which should be a good example to draw from, don't you
think? the best players all playing good decks?) shows us:

Jared Strait, playing Brujah Prince vote and combat, .5VP
Robert Goudie, playing weenie Potence rush, 1.5VP
Stephen Fazio, playing Toreador showcase, 0VP
Ben Peal, playing Malkavian Obf/Dom with Change of Target, 1.5VP (win)
Trey Morita, playing Gangrel Superior Protean something-or-other, 0VP

Trey's deck was packing 21+ S:CE cards, both Form of Mist and Earth Meld.
He got zero VPs in the final. Stephen's deck was packing 10 Majesty; he
also got zero VPs in the final. Ben had no S:CE at all. Neither did
Robert. They were the only players to oust anyone in the final. (Jared
also had no S:CE in his deck.)

Now... why don't you tell me again just how "unfair" Majesty is? It, like
every other card in the game, has an opportunity cost. If you put too many
in your deck (10 is pushing it, 21 is WELL over the line), you take a very
large risk of jamming up on them and dying miserably. Both Earth Meld and
Majesty have a strong effect at superior, but they're hardly broken, nor do
they need to be banned.

(it's worth noting that Trey's deck relied on being able to intercept LOTS
of actions in order to consistently get into combat and play his S:CE.
Anyone wishing to claim that intercept decks are broken is welcome to; i
always enjoy a good laugh.)

> to make calls on that, but it would be nice to just ban Majesty too

I wouldn't trust you to make a call to order pizza.

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
> (it's worth noting that Trey's deck relied on being able to intercept LOTS
> of actions in order to consistently get into combat and play his S:CE.
> Anyone wishing to claim that intercept decks are broken is welcome to; i
> always enjoy a good laugh.)
If Forms of Mist were part of that 21, I think he was also counting on
being blocked once in a while, too. There again, I don't know what
was in the rest of the deck, so I can't make that call accurately.

Not only is it prone to jamming, but there are SO many ways around it
now -- Thoughts Betrayed, Immortal Grapple, Psyche, Telepathic
Tracking, Guard Dogs (not that they're ever used), etc, etc. I would
think with a weenie potence deck at the table, Grapples were present
in the finals environment, and that's going to hose a S:CE deck. The
Brujah Princes deck probably had Grapple, Psyche, or both. With two
pot-based combat decks, it creates a VERY S:CE-unfriendly environment.

Powerful, yes. Broken, no.

Sadly, a dedicated intercept deck going against a dedicated stealth
deck will not block everything. Forgotten Labyrinth makes it hard for
intercept decks to keep up. Ravnos can do it most often, by reducing
stealth to zero -- but I don't think anyone would say the Ravnos are
broken. =)

Fanboy

Which is a good thing. Offense should always have a slight edge over
defense, in order to ensure that games end.

with my dedicated intercept decks. The trick is to stack up a couple
permanents until you can get a solid +2 on a vampire, then use transients
to boost it as need be; and discard the transients if you don't need them
with something like the Fraggie (which fits well in a bait deck).

Elder Impersonation, however, is a REAL bitch; especially when combined
with Faceless Night. "That vampire with the three Revenants won't EVER
block this action, and just for attempting he taps. Anyone else able to
get +2 intercept, or does this vote happen my way?"

overall argument.)

Indeed. A very useful tempering aspect to have with that perception is
that through careful and detailed discussions, you can come to more,
perhaps better, conclusions. The perception is yours; it doesn't have
to remain so.

>There is little to be done or
>can even possibly be done to change it.

Why?

Consider a person who has an attitude regarding, say, computers. All
computers are evil, work of the devil and far too complicated - perhaps
a Luddite or Amish tendency. They carry on for years and years and
years, doing everything by pen and paper, keeping all their accounts
that way. As a result of a set of circumstances, they have to go on a
computer course and find out that actually a spread-sheet has some
advantages for them because they could alter the figures for this month
and try out a few dozen scenarios for next month's figures in half an
hour. They'd be able to decide that *actually* computers weren't so bad
after all.

Having views, principles and motivations based on your experience is
great; keeping an open mind to the world around you is similarly great.
If you find that something actually is pretty good after all, keeping
your previous opinion come what may smacks of cutting off your nose to
spite your face.

Taking a Jyhad context, several years ago you could have asked anyone if
they thought Banishment was a usable card. I'd wager that just as V:TES
was coming out, or maybe onto Dark Sovereigns too, most people would be
of the opinion that Banishment was a nice flavour card but had no
significant practical uses - its opportunity cost was way too high for
too little effect. Even as Sabbat came out, this would have been the
prevailing mood.

Legbiter, however, took Banishment and managed to make a highly
effective, powerful, innovative deck. Now, this hasn't suddenly made
Banishment the be-all and end-all of cards, but it has shown that
Banishment can be used and used well. Sticking to previous opinions, in
the face of empirical evidence, would be churlish.

>There is the first amendment and
>all

It is also useful to remember that not all of the Internet is American.

For inexperienced netizens: This is a very common troll, where the troller
spins a tale to play to the imaginary crowd and appear as a helpless
victim, when actually he was the instigator. The whole idea is to somehow
drum up popular support against the Evil Meanie (that's me, here) for
somehow hurting the troller's feelings with my vile, nasty statements ("put
a sock in it") to such a great extent that his concept of V:TES is forever
tainted by its association with me, and he just COULDN'T bring himself to
play it, ever... and so one player will be forever lost to the Murky Mists
(tm), perhaps even playing that terrible M-word game instead. He then
speculates randomly about others I may have also scarred with my terrible
depradations, in hopes of stirring things up even further.

It bears a notable resemblance to classic IBM/Microsoft FUD; it's certainly
been around for that long, if not longer. I believe I first saw this troll
back when I still had a 300bps modem, in the old, old BBS days.

The reality is, almost nobody selects USENET as a first resource to get
back into V:TES. The vast majority of our new players come to us (or come
back) from in-person hookups at local gaming shops and word-of-mouth, while
some go look on White Wolf's website or the V:TES mailing list. As far as
marginal goes... We were effectively abandoned and ashcanned by WotC for
several years. Of course we're marginal. But we're taking off like a
rocket. We'll be fine, even if we lose one player. ;)

I've seen it happen at conventions - players who score 0 VP in the first
two rounds drop before the third round so that they can go play in another
event. I've even seen it happen after the first round, but usually that
only happens in a limited (judge-provides-cards) tournament at a
convention - some players will stay just long enough to get their cards
and then drop. In both cases, the bigger the convention, the more
appeal to dropping (boosted by the fact that bigger conventions lead to
more players in the tournament, which means that slow starts are more likely
to mean no final).

But I've never seen anyone drop from a "stand-alone" tournament (a tournament
held in a non-convention setting).

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
Derek Ray <lor...@yahoo.com> wrote in message news:<Xns91028ECA...@198.99.146.10>...
>
> > common thread on new errata, and it doesn't make me happy. It's just
> > a different form of card-limits.
>
> Making a card non-stackable COMPLETELY and TOTALLY fails to resemble
> anything to do with card limits. You can put as many LoP in your deck as
> you want, and put as many in play as you want, and each one must be burned
> by a separate action. You just can't stack them up to have a weenie
> powerhouse vote machine anymore. Corresponding examples: A vampire may
> have no more than one Disarm, and you can still put 12 of them in your deck
> (probably quite effectively). You can no longer play more than one DotB
> per combat, and it's STILL worth putting a bunch in.
>
It *is* similar to card limits in that it a) is an artificial
construct which limits cards which are deemed too powerful to be
played multiple times, and b) limits the effective number of uses you
can get out of the cards, similar to the way card limits do. Legacy
of Pander was a cool card in that you could base a deck around it. I
don't see that happening anymore.
And let me bring up unique cards before you do. I see that unique
cards are in the game and that the unique clause is pretty much the
same thing as this kind of errata. It mainly differs in that those
cards were always designed not to stack, and has other implications on
the game (contesting, mainly), while also being a part of the
backstory. It *does* also vaguely resemble card limits, except that I
seem to remember some talk early on that having unique cards
essentially removed the *need* for card limits.

> You would also consider the original Army of Rats errata bad?

Yes, in that it's artificially limiting. No, in that AoR is horribly
overpowered as originally printed. Unfortunately, this errata was
probably the only thing that could have been done to the card. I
don't believe that DoTB and Legacy of Pander were really overpowered.
And yes, I have seen them in action, in well-tuned decks, and while
they were good cards/combos, I was left feeling somewhat underwhelmed.
Ah well, c'est la vie. I will no longer play 6 DoTB's and an Aid
From Bats in one combat... as fun as that used to be. 8)
